documents.title: What the Banking Code of Practice is and which version applies
documents.source: Australian Banking Association – Banking Code of Practice
documents.keywords: Banking Code of Practice ABA industry code ASIC approved 2025 code Banking Code Compliance Committee customer rights What is the Banking Code of Practice? Is the Banking Code approved by the government? Who checks that banks follow the Banking Code?
questions: What is the Banking Code of Practice?
Is the Banking Code approved by the government?
Who checks that banks follow the Banking Code?
documents.text: The Banking Code of Practice is the Australian banking industry's code, published by the Australian Banking Association (ABA). The 2025 Banking Code of Practice was approved by ASIC on 27 June 2024 and is effective from 28 February 2025. The independent Banking Code Compliance Committee monitors banks' compliance with the Code. The Code replaces the version dated 5 October 2021. A 2026 Banking Code Review is underway.

documents.title: Banking Code: help for customers in financial difficulty
documents.source: Australian Banking Association – Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025)
documents.keywords: financial difficulty hardship Banking Code hardship interest only extend loan defer payments superannuation debt sold financial counsellor What does the Banking Code say about hardship? Can my bank make me use my super to pay my loan? Can the bank sell my debt while I'm in hardship?
questions: What does the Banking Code say about hardship?
Can my bank make me use my super to pay my loan?
Can the bank sell my debt while I'm in hardship?
documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), Financial Difficulty means being unable to repay what you owe, expecting to be unable to pay upcoming repayments, or having difficulty meeting repayment obligations. Examples of help include short-term interest-only payments, extending the loan term to reduce repayments, or temporarily postponing or deferring payments, which may increase total interest. The bank will tell the customer in writing whether it will help and the reasons for its decision. Customers can ask the bank to deal with their financial counsellor or representative. The bank will not require a customer to access superannuation to repay a loan (unless borrowing for a self-managed super fund), and will not sell the debt while actively considering the customer's financial situation.

documents.title: Banking Code: protections for guarantors
documents.source: Australian Banking Association – Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025)
documents.keywords: guarantor guarantee parents guaranteeing loan go guarantor family guarantee cooling off legal advice borrower default My son wants me to be guarantor on his home loan, what protections do I have? Does the bank have to meet me before I sign as guarantor? Will the bank tell me if the borrower stops paying?
questions: My son wants me to be guarantor on his home loan, what protections do I have?
Does the bank have to meet me before I sign as guarantor?
Will the bank tell me if the borrower stops paying?
documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), before accepting a guarantee the bank will take reasonable steps to hold a meeting with the prospective guarantor, in person or by video, phone or other means, without the borrower present, unless the guarantor has received independent legal advice or another exception applies. The bank will not accept a guarantee until the third day after the guarantor has been given the required information, unless an exception applies. Within 14 days of the relevant event, the bank will send the guarantor copies of formal demands or default notices, and notices about borrower hardship changes or a continuing default of more than two months.

documents.source: Australian Banking Association – Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025)
documents.keywords: accessibility disability interpreter Auslan National Relay Service First Nations ID requirements limited English older customers concession card low fee account Does the bank have to provide an interpreter for free? documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), banks will take reasonable measures to make their services accessible, including for older customers, people with disability, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customers and people with limited English. Where practicable, banks will organise or refer customers to free external support, including interpreter services (including Auslan) and the National Relay Service. Banks will help Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customers meet identification requirements when they lack standard ID documents, following AUSTRAC's guidance. Customers who tell the bank they hold a Commonwealth Seniors Health Card, Health Care Card or Pensioner Concession Card will be given information about basic, low-fee or no-fee accounts.

documents.title: Banking Code: extra care for customers experiencing vulnerability
documents.source: Australian Banking Association – Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025)
documents.keywords: vulnerable extra care elder abuse domestic violence financial abuse mental health disability tell the bank my situation Does the bank have to take extra care if I'm going through a hard time? What does the Banking Code say about elder abuse? Should I tell my bank about my mental health issues?

What does the Banking Code say about elder abuse?
Should I tell my bank about my mental health issues?
documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), banks commit to taking extra care with customers who are experiencing vulnerability. Circumstances the Code lists include age, disability, mental health conditions, elder abuse, family and/or domestic violence, financial abuse, Financial Difficulty and language barriers. The Code encourages customers to tell their bank about their circumstances so the bank can provide appropriate support.

documents.title: Banking Code: deceased estates
documents.source: Australian Banking Association – Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025)
documents.keywords: deceased estate someone died bereavement executor fees after death funeral expenses 14 business days before probate How quickly must a bank act on an executor's instructions? Can the bank keep charging fees on my late father's account? Can funeral costs be paid from the account before probate?
questions: How quickly must a bank act on an executor's instructions?
Can the bank keep charging fees on my late father's account?
Can funeral costs be paid from the account before probate?
documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), once a bank has received the verified documents it needs, it will act on a valid Deceased Estate Representative instruction about a deceased's accounts within 14 business days. For accounts in the deceased's sole name, the bank will promptly identify and stop charging fees for banking services that can no longer be provided. Before probate, a representative can still request account information and give instructions to release funds to pay or reimburse permissible expenses such as funeral expenses.

documents.title: Banking Code: who counts as a small business
documents.source: Australian Banking Association – Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025)
documents.keywords: small business business customer Banking Code small business definition turnover employees business loan Does the Banking Code protect my small business? What counts as a small business under the Banking Code? Is my company covered by the Banking Code?
questions: Does the Banking Code protect my small business?
What counts as a small business under the Banking Code?
Is my company covered by the Banking Code?
documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), a business is a Small Business if it, together with any related entities, had an annual turnover of less than $10 million in the previous financial year, has fewer than 100 full-time equivalent employees, and has less than $5 million total debt to all credit providers. Small Business customers receive the Code's protections alongside individual customers.

documents.title: Your legal right to ask any lender for financial hardship help
documents.keywords: hardship rights can't pay struggling with repayments lender must consider hardship request refused hardship ask early Does my bank have to help me if I can't pay my loan? What are my rights if I'm in financial hardship? Can the bank refuse my hardship request?
questions: Does my bank have to help me if I can't pay my loan?
What are my rights if I'm in financial hardship?
Can the bank refuse my hardship request?
documents.text: Moneysmart, the Australian Government's financial guidance service run by ASIC, says that when a borrower asks for help, the lender must consider them for hardship assistance. Borrowers can contact the lender's hardship team by phone, email or chat, and Moneysmart says the earlier you seek help, the more options you will have. Hardship help can be temporary, such as deferring a payment, or permanent, such as varying the loan. Moneysmart says a lender must give reasons if it refuses a request for hardship assistance, and the borrower can then complain.

documents.title: How long a lender has to respond to a hardship notice under the National Credit Code
documents.source: ASIC – INFO 105 Dealing with consumers and credit (updated May 2025)
documents.keywords: hardship notice 21 days 28 days response time how long does the bank have National Credit Code section 72 hardship decision How long does the bank legally have to answer my hardship request? Is there a deadline for the lender to respond to hardship? Can I ask for hardship verbally or does it need to be in writing?
tags: how long does the bank have
questions: How long does the bank legally have to answer my hardship request?
Is there a deadline for the lender to respond to hardship?
Can I ask for hardship verbally or does it need to be in writing?
documents.text: Under section 72 of the National Credit Code, a borrower can give their credit provider a hardship notice, verbally or in writing, saying they cannot meet their obligations. ASIC's INFO 105 (updated May 2025) says that if the lender has enough information it must tell the borrower its decision within 21 days, starting the day after it receives the notice. If it needs more information it must ask within 21 days; it then has 21 days from receiving the information to respond, or 28 days from its request if the information is not provided. If the lender does not agree to change the contract, it must give its reasons and the contact details of the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).

documents.text: ASIC's INFO 105 (updated May 2025) says that under the National Credit Code, if an agreed hardship change defers or reduces the borrower's obligations for more than 90 days, the credit provider must give the borrower written notice of the changes no later than 30 days after the date of the agreement.

documents.text: The National Debt Helpline offers free and confidential financial counselling for people struggling with debt. Call 1800 007 007; phone lines are open weekdays 9:30am to 4:30pm, and live chat is available weekdays 9:00am to 8:00pm.

documents.title: Lender must pause enforcement after a first hardship notice
documents.source: National Debt Helpline – What is financial hardship and what are your rights
documents.keywords: debt collection legal action repossession enforcement stop the bank suing me hardship notice 21 to 30 days Can the bank take legal action while my hardship request is being considered? Will the bank repossess my house if I ask for hardship? How long does a lender have to respond to hardship?
questions: Can the bank take legal action while my hardship request is being considered?
Will the bank repossess my house if I ask for hardship?
How long does a lender have to respond to hardship?
documents.text: The National Debt Helpline says a lender has between 21 and 30 days to respond to a hardship request, depending on whether it asks for more information. The first time a borrower gives a hardship notice in a three-month period, the lender must stop further enforcement or legal action until it responds. This protection does not apply if the lender already has a court judgment. If the lender refuses the hardship request, the borrower can lodge a free dispute with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).

documents.title: Maximum time a bank has to respond to a complaint (ASIC RG 271)
documents.source: ASIC – Regulatory Guide 271 Internal dispute resolution
documents.keywords: complaint deadline 30 days 21 days how long does the bank have to respond maximum timeframe IDR acknowledge complaint hardship complaint How many days does a bank legally have to respond to a complaint? What is the maximum time for a bank to resolve a hardship complaint? The bank hasn't replied to my complaint in a month, is that allowed?
tags: how long does the bank have to respond
questions: How many days does a bank legally have to respond to a complaint?
What is the maximum time for a bank to resolve a hardship complaint?
The bank hasn't replied to my complaint in a month, is that allowed?
documents.text: ASIC Regulatory Guide 271 sets enforceable internal dispute resolution (IDR) standards for banks and other financial firms, for complaints received from 5 October 2021. ASIC expects firms to acknowledge a complaint within 24 hours (or one business day), or as soon as practicable. A bank must give its IDR response no later than 30 calendar days after receiving a standard complaint. For credit complaints involving default notices, hardship notices or requests to postpone enforcement, the maximum is 21 calendar days. If a bank cannot meet the deadline because the complaint is particularly complex or circumstances are beyond its control, it must send an IDR delay notification before the deadline giving the reasons, the right to go to AFCA, and AFCA's contact details.

documents.title: What a bank's final complaint response must include (ASIC RG 271)
documents.source: ASIC – Regulatory Guide 271 Internal dispute resolution
documents.keywords: final response IDR response complaint rejected reasons written response right to AFCA what counts as a complaint What should the bank's final response to my complaint include? The bank rejected my complaint without explaining why, is that allowed? What counts as a complaint?
questions: What should the bank's final response to my complaint include?
The bank rejected my complaint without explaining why, is that allowed?
What counts as a complaint?
documents.text: Under ASIC Regulatory Guide 271, a complaint is any expression of dissatisfaction about a firm's products, services, staff or complaint handling where a response or resolution is expected. A bank's IDR response must be in writing and tell the customer the final outcome, their right to take the complaint to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), and AFCA's contact details. If the complaint is rejected or partly rejected, the response must clearly set out the reasons, identify and address the issues raised, and set out the bank's findings on material questions of fact.

documents.title: AFCA: free external complaints after your bank
documents.keywords: AFCA ombudsman external dispute resolution free escalate take bank to ombudsman lodge complaint online phone number What is AFCA and does it cost anything? How do I take my complaint further than the bank? What are AFCA's phone hours?

documents.text: Moneysmart says the first step in any complaint is to contact the business, explain the problem and say how you would like it fixed. If the bank does not respond in a reasonable time, or the customer is unhappy with its handling or offer, they can complain to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA). AFCA is an independent dispute resolution scheme for disputes with financial firms, including banking, credit and loans, and it hears complaints for free. AFCA can be contacted on 1800 931 678 (9am to 5pm, Monday to Friday) or online at www.afca.org.au. AFCA's time limits and compensation caps are not covered in this knowledge base; check afca.org.au.

documents.title: The ePayments Code: who it covers
documents.keywords: ePayments Code electronic payments voluntary code ATM EFTPOS online banking BPAY consumer protection What is the ePayments Code? Does the ePayments Code apply to my bank? What protections do I have for online banking payments?
questions: What is the ePayments Code?
Does the ePayments Code apply to my bank?
What protections do I have for online banking payments?
documents.text: The ePayments Code is a code of practice administered by ASIC, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. ASIC describes it as presently a voluntary code, and most banks, credit unions and building societies subscribe to it. The ePayments Code covers electronic payments such as ATM, EFTPOS and credit card transactions, online and mobile banking, and BPAY. The current version has applied since 2 June 2022. It sets rules on who pays for unauthorised transactions and how mistaken internet payments are handled.

documents.title: Who pays for unauthorised transactions under the ePayments Code
documents.keywords: unauthorised transaction not my transaction who is liable money taken from my account $150 passcode fraud refund card stolen Do I have to pay for transactions I didn't authorise? Is the bank responsible if someone stole money from my account? What's the most I can lose if my card was used without permission?
questions: Do I have to pay for transactions I didn't authorise?
Is the bank responsible if someone stole money from my account?
What's the most I can lose if my card was used without permission?
documents.text: Under the ePayments Code (effective 2 June 2022), an account holder is not liable for an unauthorised transaction where it is clear the user did not contribute to the loss, or where the loss was caused by fraud or negligence of bank staff or merchants, forged, faulty, expired or cancelled cards or passcodes, transactions before the card or passcode was received, duplicate debits, or transactions after loss or theft was reported. The bank must prove on the balance of probability that the user contributed through fraud or a passcode security breach, and a breach alone is not enough. Where a passcode was required and no other rule applies, liability is limited to the least of $150 (or lower), the available balance, or the actual loss when reported.

documents.title: Reporting delays and your liability under the ePayments Code
documents.keywords: report quickly delay reporting lost card unauthorised transaction reference number contact bank How quickly do I need to report an unauthorised transaction? Will I be liable if I report fraud late? What should I do if I see a transaction I don't recognise?
questions: How quickly do I need to report an unauthorised transaction?
Will I be liable if I report fraud late?
What should I do if I see a transaction I don't recognise?
documents.text: Under the ePayments Code (effective 2 June 2022), a user who unreasonably delays reporting a lost or stolen card or device, or a compromised passcode, can be liable for losses that occur during the delay, subject to transaction limits. An account holder is not liable for losses from unauthorised transactions that happen after the user has reported the loss, theft or misuse of the card or device, or the breach of passcode security.

documents.title: Mistaken payment to the wrong account: how to get money back
documents.keywords: wrong account mistaken payment typo in account number sent money to wrong person wrong BSB get money back 10 business days 7 months I sent money to the wrong account number, can I get it back? What happens if I paid the wrong person by mistake? Is there a time limit to recover a mistaken payment?
questions: I sent money to the wrong account number, can I get it back?
What happens if I paid the wrong person by mistake?
Is there a time limit to recover a mistaken payment?
documents.text: Under the ePayments Code (effective 2 June 2022), a mistaken internet payment should be reported to your own bank, and the process depends on when it is reported. Within 10 business days, if the funds are available, the receiving bank must return them within 5 business days if practicable and no later than 10 business days, without needing the recipient's consent. Between 10 business days and 7 months, the receiving bank investigates within 10 business days and, if satisfied, freezes the funds for 10 further business days, returning them unless the recipient proves they are entitled to them. After 7 months, funds are returned only if the unintended recipient consents.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), a customer can complain about a bank's banking services or its compliance with the Code. If a bank that subscribes to the Code cannot resolve a complaint within 30 days, or 21 days if it involves a hardship notice, default notice or request to postpone enforcement under the National Credit Code, the bank will tell the customer the reasons for the delay and the date by which they can reasonably expect to hear the outcome, give monthly progress updates, and tell them about the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).

documents.text: Moneysmart says you have a right to get a copy of your credit report for free every 3 months, or more often if you have recently been rejected for credit. Moneysmart names Experian and Equifax as the two main credit reporting bodies. Defaults stay on a credit report for five years, or seven years for a clearout, and repayment history covers the last two years. Getting errors on a credit report fixed is a free service.

documents.text: Under Australia's responsible lending obligations, administered by ASIC, credit licensees such as banks must not enter into a credit contract that is unsuitable for the consumer. They must make reasonable inquiries about the consumer's financial situation and their requirements and objectives, take reasonable steps to verify the consumer's financial situation, and assess that the contract is "not unsuitable". The consumer can request a written copy of the assessment.

documents.text: ASIC, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, says money from old bank accounts that a bank cannot return to the owner after seven years of inactivity is held by ASIC if it is more than $500, while claims related to old bank accounts under $500 should be made with the bank. People can search for unclaimed money using ASIC's free Moneysmart search tool. ASIC says the search and claims process is completely free, and there is no deadline to make a claim.

documents.title: Scams Prevention Framework: new legal duties for banks
documents.keywords: Scams Prevention Framework scam law bank responsibility for scams compensation for scams new scam rules 2027 AFCA scam complaints Are banks now legally required to protect me from scams? When do the new scam laws start? Can I complain to AFCA if my bank didn't stop a scam?

documents.text: ASIC says the Scams Prevention Framework imposes enforceable obligations on banks and other regulated businesses to prevent, detect, disrupt, report and respond to scams. Most Scams Prevention Framework obligations commence on 31 March 2027. The Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) is the external dispute resolution scheme for Scams Prevention Framework complaints, and covered businesses had to be AFCA members by 1 September 2026. AFCA is a free and independent dispute resolution service.

documents.title: What to do if you've been scammed (Moneysmart)
documents.source: Moneysmart (ASIC) – What to do if you've been scammed
documents.keywords: scammed lost money to scam what to do report scam Scamwatch IDCARE change passwords recovery scam get money back I've been scammed, what steps should I take? Can I get my money back after a scam? Someone says they can recover my scam losses for a fee, is that real?
questions: I've been scammed, what steps should I take?

documents.text: Moneysmart says anyone who has been scammed should contact their bank or card provider immediately to report the scam, report the scam to Scamwatch to help protect others, change passwords, and contact IDCARE on 1800 595 160 for a free response plan. Moneysmart warns to be wary of anyone who claims they can recover your losses for a percentage of the recovered losses, as this is a common follow-up scam. If unhappy with the bank's response, the customer can make a formal complaint to the bank and then to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).

documents.title: Westpac and the Banking Code of Practice
documents.keywords: Banking Code of Practice code of conduct ABA industry code customer rights 2025 code legally binding guarantor Does Westpac follow the Banking Code of Practice? Which version of the Banking Code applies to me? Is the Banking Code legally binding on Westpac?

documents.text: Westpac says it is committed to upholding the Australian banking industry's standards of practice and service set out in the Banking Code of Practice. The current version of the Code took effect on 28 February 2025 and replaced the 2019 Code, which still applies to certain agreements made before that date. The Code covers individual and small business customers and their individual guarantors. Where the Code applies, Westpac describes it as a legally binding agreement between Westpac and its customers.

documents.text: Westpac says money in a bank account is considered "unclaimed" when the account has a balance of $500 or more and there have been no customer deposits or withdrawals for 7 years or longer. Interest earned and fees charged do not count as activity. Westpac must close these accounts and send the funds to ASIC by 31 March each year. To reclaim the money, search ASIC's Moneysmart unclaimed money tool, note the Original Transaction Number, and take the completed claim form to a Westpac branch with two forms of ID (one with a photo) and proof of account ownership. Westpac says the process can take up to 3 months.

documents.text: Under Westpac's Personal Accounts Terms and Conditions (effective 27 August 2026), a personal deposit account becomes inactive if there are no deposits or withdrawals for a continuous six months and the balance is nil, or in debit without an arrangement; Westpac may close an inactive account without notice. Westpac may also close an account after giving reasonable notice, for example for unsatisfactory conduct, business use of a personal account, or where it reasonably believes the account's use has caused harm, such as financial abuse, to another person. In some cases it may act without prior notice, but Westpac says it will act fairly and reasonably.

documents.text: The Financial Claims Scheme (FCS) is an Australian Government scheme that, if activated after a bank fails, protects certain deposits up to $250,000 per account holder per eligible authorised deposit-taking institution (ADI). APRA administers the FCS and aims to pay most customers within seven calendar days. Westpac, St.George, Bank of Melbourne and BankSA all operate under one Westpac banking licence, so a customer's combined deposits across those brands, plus eligible Westpac products sold under third-party brands, share one $250,000 limit.

documents.text: Westpac's Personal Accounts Terms and Conditions (effective 27 August 2026) say Westpac will always let customers know if the terms and conditions of their account change. Westpac gives at least 30 days' notice of a new or increased fee and of changes it believes are unfavourable to the customer. Advance notice may not be given where a change is needed immediately to restore or maintain security, or to manage a material and immediate risk. Interest rate changes are notified no later than the day of the change, except where the rate is linked to money market or other rates. Notice may be in writing, electronically or by media advertisement.

Questions about a deceased person's home loan go to 132 558. Westpac's support guide (April 2026) asks for a completed Deceased Customer Notification & Estate Form and one document confirming the death, such as a death certificate, medical or police report, or probate or letters of administration. documents.text: Westpac says anyone can let Westpac know when someone has died, including through deathnotification.gov.au if the death was registered in Australia. Only the next of kin, the executor or a legal representative of the estate can manage the estate. After notification, sole accounts in the deceased's name are restrained, which stops direct debits and recurring payments, although deposits can still be received. Loan repayments must continue and interest will still accrue. Joint account holders keep access to joint accounts as usual.

documents.text: Westpac's deceased estates support guide (April 2026) says a Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration is required if the estate balance with Westpac is $100,000 or more, if the estate includes secured lending, or if an "Estate of the Late" account is wanted (that account can only be set up in a branch). Simpler documents apply below $100,000 with no secured lending. Westpac can pay the funeral director directly from the estate once it has the funeral invoice. Once Westpac has all required documents, it completes estate instructions within 14 business days.

documents.text: Westpac recognises three ways a trusted person can help with banking. A power of attorney (general or enduring) is set up through an in-branch process, with legal paperwork and an appointment required; an enduring power of attorney must be set up while the person still has capacity to make decisions. An account signatory can operate the account, set up in a branch. An authorised third party, such as a financial counsellor, can speak with Westpac by phone but does not have direct access to the customer's accounts.

documents.text: Westpac offers financial hardship assistance to customers who are struggling to make their repayments. Westpac says the options it may tailor include flexible payment arrangements, short-term deferrals or repayment reductions, and loan term extensions. Westpac assesses assistance on a case by case basis, so the option offered depends on the customer's circumstances. Customers can apply online, which Westpac says can take as little as 15 minutes, or call the Westpac Assist team on 1800 067 497.

Before applying, Westpac suggests having ready: current income and expenses; what you owe, including loans and credit cards with Westpac and other institutions; and what you own. Westpac's hardship pages list Westpac Assist hours as Monday to Friday 8:30am to 8:00pm and Saturday 9:30am to 6pm, Sydney time.

documents.text: Westpac's hardship support covers customers with a Westpac home loan, personal loan or credit card. For online financial hardship applications, Westpac says it aims to get back to the customer within a week. If a customer is unhappy with Westpac's response to a hardship request, Westpac's hardship page points them to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), a free external dispute resolution service: phone 1800 931 678, website www.afca.org.au, email info@afca.org.au.

Customers who are unsure whether they can meet revised repayments can talk to the Westpac Assist team on 1800 067 497.

documents.text: Westpac's Privacy Statement (effective August 2026) says Westpac collects personal and contact details; government identification such as Medicare number, passport details and driver's licence number, and copies of ID documents; call recordings when customers contact call centres or branches; transaction records; and device and app data such as device IDs and IP addresses. documents.text: Westpac's Credit Reporting Policy, part of its Privacy Statement (effective August 2026), says Westpac uses two credit reporting bodies: Equifax (13 83 32, equifax.com.au) and Experian (1300 783 684, experian.com.au). Would Westpac ask for remote access to my computer?
documents.text: Westpac's online banking scam and fraud flyer says Westpac will never send links requesting personal or financial information, never ask customers to share their password or Security Code, never ask customers to install software that connects to their device, and never send a link that directly opens the Westpac sign-in page. A message or caller doing any of these is a warning sign of a scam, and it should be reported to Westpac through the Westpac App, Online Banking, or 1300 364 294.

documents.title: What Westpac does after you report a card scam or fraud
documents.source: Westpac – Card scam and fraud flyer (WL1767 05/25)
documents.keywords: card fraud card investigation how long refund replacement card Fraud Money Back Guarantee unauthorised card transaction chargeback How long does a Westpac card fraud investigation take? Will Westpac refund fraudulent charges on my card? What happens after I report card fraud?
questions: How long does a Westpac card fraud investigation take?
Will Westpac refund fraudulent charges on my card?
What happens after I report card fraud?
documents.text: After a card scam or fraud is reported, Westpac says it will attempt to stop transactions where it can intervene, cancel and replace compromised cards, and confirm the case by email or SMS; a Digital Card is available in the Westpac App while waiting. Card fraud investigations normally take 21 days, and more complex cases up to 45 days. Under the Westpac Fraud Money Back Guarantee, customers are reimbursed for unauthorised card transactions provided they have not contributed to the loss and contacted Westpac promptly; the card's conditions of use set out when the customer is liable.

documents.title: Westpac Online Banking Security Guarantee and online banking fraud investigations
documents.source: Westpac – Online banking scam and fraud flyer (WL1766 05/25)
documents.keywords: online banking hacked account compromised internet fraud refund money back Online Banking Security Guarantee investigation time recover funds Someone hacked my online banking, will I get my money back? How long does an online banking fraud investigation take? Will Westpac try to recover money I sent to a scammer?
questions: Someone hacked my online banking, will I get my money back?
How long does an online banking fraud investigation take?
Will Westpac try to recover money I sent to a scammer?
documents.text: After an online banking scam or fraud is reported, Westpac says it may stop payments, attempt to recover funds by reporting the transactions to other financial institutions, and reset the customer's Online or Telephone Banking password. Banking may remain blocked during the investigation if reinstating access would expose the customer to further loss. Standard cases take up to 21 days and complex cases may take longer. If the customer is eligible for a refund under the Westpac Online Banking Security Guarantee, Westpac credits the funds back to the account they were debited from. Case updates: westpac.com.au/scamcase or 1300 364 294.

documents.title: Westpac Online Banking Security Guarantee conditions
documents.keywords: guarantee conditions eligible for refund keep password private shared my code report immediately Online Banking Security Guarantee When does Westpac's online banking guarantee not apply? Do I get my money back if I gave the scammer my code? What do I have to do to be covered by the Westpac guarantee?
questions: When does Westpac's online banking guarantee not apply?
Do I get my money back if I gave the scammer my code?
What do I have to do to be covered by the Westpac guarantee?
documents.text: Under the Westpac Online Banking Security Guarantee, if a Westpac account is compromised as a result of internet fraud, Westpac guarantees to repay any missing funds, provided the customer complies with Westpac's Online Banking Terms and Conditions. This includes keeping sign-in details, such as passwords, Westpac Protect SMS codes and SecurID token codes, private. The customer must also tell Westpac immediately if they suspect their access details have been compromised or suspect an unauthorised transaction or potential fraud. Westpac says the guarantee does not apply to Corporate Online Banking.

documents.title: SafeBlock: lock all your Westpac accounts and cards
documents.keywords: SafeBlock lock accounts freeze account block my account shared details with scammer emergency lock card lock How do I freeze all my Westpac accounts if I've been scammed? What does SafeBlock stop? I gave my details to a scammer, can I lock everything?
questions: How do I freeze all my Westpac accounts if I've been scammed?
What does SafeBlock stop?
I gave my details to a scammer, can I lock everything?
documents.text: Westpac SafeBlock is a security feature customers can use in the Westpac App or Online Banking (search "SafeBlock") if they suspect fraud or think they have shared details with a scammer. It instantly locks the customer's accounts and cards. SafeBlock blocks new Online Banking payments and transfers, new card purchases, ATM withdrawals and most recurring card payments. It does not stop deposits, direct debits, scheduled payments set up with an account number, branch transactions or telephone banking. Unlocking may require identity verification and can take time.

questions: I lost my card, can I lock it temporarily?
How long does a Westpac card lock last?
How do I cancel a stolen Westpac card?
documents.text: Westpac customers can temporarily lock a card in the Westpac App for up to 15 days while they look for it: search "Lock card" and tap "Lock/Unlock card temporarily". The card unlocks automatically after 15 days. To permanently cancel a lost or stolen card and order a replacement, the customer should report it as lost or stolen in the Westpac App or Online Banking instead of locking it.

documents.title: Westpac Verify and Confirmation of Payee when paying someone new
documents.keywords: Confirmation of Payee Westpac Verify name doesn't match new payee BSB and account number details don't match wrong account payment check What does "details don't match" mean when paying someone? Does Westpac check the account name matches? Can I opt out of Confirmation of Payee?
questions: What does "details don't match" mean when paying someone?
Does Westpac check the account name matches?
Can I opt out of Confirmation of Payee?
documents.text: When paying someone new by BSB and account number, Westpac Verify with Confirmation of Payee checks the details against the receiving bank's records and Westpac's payment data. Results include "Everything checks out", "Details don't match", "Worth a second look" and "Try again later". If the details don't match, Westpac advises calling the payee to confirm the details and warns that if money is sent to the wrong account it may not be able to recover the funds. The check is only available in Westpac Online Banking and the Westpac App. Eligible individual and sole trader customers can request to opt out of Confirmation of Payee.

documents.title: Westpac SaferPay and payment delays to new payees
documents.keywords: SaferPay payment stopped payment blocked payment held extra questions scam check why was my payment stopped Why did Westpac stop my payment? Westpac asked me questions about my payment, why? My transfer was blocked as a possible scam
questions: Why did Westpac stop my payment?
Westpac asked me questions about my payment, why?
My transfer was blocked as a possible scam
documents.text: Westpac SaferPay asks the customer extra questions when a payment shows signs of a scam. If the answers raise concerns, Westpac will prevent the money from leaving the account, and a payment Westpac has categorised as consistent with scam activity will not be processed. Westpac also says payments may take longer when paying a first-time payee or when a payment is caught for additional security screening, and paying someone for the first time usually requires a Security Code. Westpac does not publish a fixed hold period for these payments.

documents.title: Disputing a card transaction with Westpac
documents.keywords: dispute chargeback charged twice didn't receive goods refund not received wrong amount merchant dispute report this transaction pending transaction How do I dispute a charge on my card? I was charged twice by a merchant, what can I do? How long does a Westpac card dispute take?
questions: How do I dispute a charge on my card?
I was charged twice by a merchant, what can I do?
How long does a Westpac card dispute take?
documents.text: Westpac suggests contacting the merchant first, because most issues are resolved more quickly that way. To lodge a card dispute, select the transaction in the Westpac App or Online Banking and choose "Report this transaction", or call 132 032 and ask to lodge a card dispute. Supporting documents can be uploaded. Pending transactions cannot be disputed until they have processed, which usually takes up to 5 business days. Westpac says disputes are usually resolved within 45 days of receiving the information needed, and it may apply a temporary credit while a dispute is reviewed.

documents.title: Chargeback time limits on Westpac Debit Mastercard
documents.source: Westpac – Debit Mastercard Terms and Conditions (effective 27 August 2026)
documents.keywords: chargeback time limit 120 days too late to dispute BPAY debit card dispute card scheme rules Is there a time limit to dispute a debit card transaction? Can I get a chargeback on a BPAY payment? I noticed a wrong charge from 3 months ago, can I still dispute it?
questions: Is there a time limit to dispute a debit card transaction?
Can I get a chargeback on a BPAY payment?
I noticed a wrong charge from 3 months ago, can I still dispute it?
documents.text: Westpac's Debit Mastercard Terms and Conditions (effective 27 August 2026) say a chargeback is when Westpac charges a disputed transaction back to the merchant under card scheme rules. Mastercard's rules require notice within 120 days of the transaction, so customers should contact Westpac as soon as possible; late notice may prevent Westpac investigating within card scheme time limits. These timeframes may not apply where the ePayments Code applies. Chargebacks are not available for all transactions; for example, Westpac cannot claim a chargeback for BPAY payments. Time limits for other card types were not checked for this knowledge base.

documents.title: Liability for unauthorised Westpac debit card transactions
documents.source: Westpac – Debit Mastercard Terms and Conditions (effective 27 August 2026)
documents.keywords: unauthorised transaction who pays liable shared my PIN wrote PIN on card $150 card stolen not my transaction Do I have to pay for transactions I didn't make on my debit card? Am I liable if I told my brother my PIN? What is the most I can lose from an unauthorised transaction?
questions: Do I have to pay for transactions I didn't make on my debit card?
Am I liable if I told my brother my PIN?
What is the most I can lose from an unauthorised transaction?
documents.text: Under Westpac's Debit Mastercard Terms and Conditions (effective 27 August 2026), the account holder is not liable for unauthorised transactions where it is clear the user has not contributed to the loss, including transactions after Westpac was told the card was lost, stolen or misused. The account holder can be liable where the user engaged in fraud, voluntarily disclosed a code to anyone (including a family member or friend), wrote the PIN on the card, acted with extreme carelessness in protecting codes, or unreasonably delayed reporting. Where a code was required and it is unclear whether the user contributed, liability is limited to the least of $150, the account balance including pre-arranged credit, or the actual loss when Westpac is notified.
